slides.title: From World War I to World War II
slides.cap: Historical connection: Unresolved postwar settlement
slides.body: World War II grew from the unstable peace that followed World War I. The Treaty of Versailles, economic crisis, wounded nationalism, and the failure of collective security gave revisionist powers room to overturn the postwar order. Germany's invasion of Poland transformed those unresolved tensions into another global war.

stats.lbl: World War II grew from the unstable peace that followed World War I. The Treaty of Versailles, economic crisis, wounded nationalism, and the failure of collective security gave revisionist powers room to overturn the postwar order. Germany's invasion of Poland transformed those unresolved tensions into another global war.

slides.title: Blitzkrieg Unleashed
slides.body: At 4:45 AM on 1 September 1939, Germany launched the most devastating military offensive Europe had ever seen. Over 1.5 million Wehrmacht soldiers crossed the Polish border simultaneously from three directions, inaugurating a new era of mechanised warfare that would define the conflict.
slides.cap: Historical connection: Unresolved postwar settlement

slides.title: Poland Encircled
slides.body: The Polish Air Force was largely destroyed within days. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east under the secret Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, completing Poland's encirclement. Despite fierce resistance in Warsaw, the nation was fighting two superpowers simultaneously.
slides.cap: Historical connection: Unresolved postwar settlement

slides.title: The World Responds
slides.body: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September — but aid came too late for Poland. Warsaw fell on the 27th. Poland was partitioned between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, vanishing once more from the map of Europe.
slides.cap: Historical connection: Unresolved postwar settlement

markers.label: Westerplatte
markers.description: Westerplatte marks the first German attack of the invasion of Poland.

markers.label: Warsaw
markers.description: Warsaw marks the Polish capital, besieged and bombed before surrendering in September 1939.

markers.label: Brest-Litovsk
markers.description: Brest-Litovsk marks eastern Poland, where German and Soviet occupation zones met.

markers.label: Dunkirk
markers.description: Dunkirk marks the evacuation point for trapped Allied armies during the fall of France.

slides.title: Blitzkrieg in the West
slides.body: In May 1940 Germany launched a lightning offensive through Belgium and the Ardennes Forest, bypassing France's heavily fortified Maginot Line. Allied commanders believed the terrain was impassable to tanks — a catastrophic miscalculation.
slides.cap: French troops setting barricades in Paris

stats.lbl: Time it took France to collapse

slides.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
slides.body: Hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers became trapped on the beaches around Dunkirk. In a desperate evacuation, civilian boats joined Royal Navy vessels to rescue over 330,000 British and French troops across the English Channel.
slides.cap: French troops setting barricades in Paris

slides.title: France Falls
slides.body: Paris fell on 14 June 1940. Days later France signed an armistice with Germany. Britain now stood alone against Nazi Germany as Hitler prepared for the next stage of the war.
slides.cap: French troops setting barricades in Paris

markers.label: London
markers.description: London marks the political center and the main target of the Blitz.

markers.label: Calais
markers.description: Calais marks the Luftwaffe's forward approach area across the Channel from Britain.

markers.label: Dover
markers.description: Dover marks Britain's Channel gateway and a key front-line air defense area.

slides.title: The Air Campaign Begins
slides.body: In August 1940 the Luftwaffe launched its main offensive against Britain, targeting RAF radar stations and airfields in an attempt to destroy Fighter Command on the ground and in the air. It was the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces — and the RAF was badly outnumbered from the start.
slides.cap: RAF station under attack during Battle of Britain

slides.title: The Blitz
slides.body: Frustrated by the RAF's resilience, Hitler shifted targeting to British cities. London was bombed for 57 consecutive nights. But the switch saved Fighter Command — and cost Germany any chance of air supremacy. Britain endured. Churchill called it their finest hour.
slides.cap: RAF station under attack during Battle of Britain

slides.title: The Largest Invasion in History
slides.body: On 22 June 1941 Germany launched Operation Barbarossa, invading the Soviet Union along a front stretching nearly 3,000 kilometres. Hitler believed the USSR could be defeated within months.
slides.cap: German soldiers inspect a downed Soviet plane during the early days of Barbarossa

slides.title: Rapid German Advances
slides.body: German forces encircled massive Soviet armies and captured hundreds of thousands of prisoners. Entire Soviet regions collapsed under the speed and violence of the assault.
slides.cap: German soldiers inspect a downed Soviet plane during the early days of Barbarossa

slides.title: The Soviet Union Endures
slides.body: Despite catastrophic losses, the Soviet Union refused to collapse. As winter arrived outside Moscow, German offensives stalled. The Eastern Front would become the largest and deadliest theater of the war.
slides.cap: German soldiers inspect a downed Soviet plane during the early days of Barbarossa

markers.label: Germany / Berlin
markers.description: Germany is marked as the launching power for Operation Barbarossa.

markers.label: Warsaw
markers.description: Warsaw marks the occupied Polish corridor through which German forces moved east.

markers.label: Minsk
markers.description: Minsk was an early major encirclement and gateway into Soviet territory.

markers.label: Kyiv
markers.description: Kyiv marks the southern axis and one of the largest encirclements of 1941.

markers.label: Smolensk
markers.description: Smolensk was a key stage on the central route toward Moscow.

markers.label: Leningrad
markers.description: Leningrad marks the northern objective and the beginning of the long siege.

markers.label: Moscow
markers.description: Moscow was the central objective where the German advance stalled in winter 1941.

title: Pearl Harbour
sub: A Date Which Will Live in Infamy

markers.label: Pearl Harbour
markers.description: Pearl Harbour marks the U.S. Pacific Fleet base attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941.

slides.title: The Sleeping Giant
slides.body: At 7:48 AM on 7 December 1941, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft launched from six carriers struck the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbour. The strike force had sailed in total radio silence across 3,400 miles of open Pacific — a feat of operational secrecy without parallel.
slides.cap: The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor

slides.title: Battleship Row
slides.body: Eight US battleships were damaged or destroyed. The USS Arizona exploded catastrophically when a bomb pierced her forward ammunition magazine, killing 1,177 of her crew. The wreck remains a war grave, still leaking oil — what locals call her 'black tears'.
slides.cap: The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor

slides.title: America Awakens
slides.body: The following day, President Roosevelt addressed Congress. His 'Day of Infamy' speech lasted seven minutes. War was declared within hours. Three days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States — transforming a European conflict into a truly global war.
slides.cap: The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor

stats.lbl: Time for Congress to declare war

slides.title: Hitler's Obsession
slides.body: Stalingrad — a city bearing Stalin's name on the Volga River — became the focal point of Germany's 1942 summer offensive. What began as a strategic objective became an ideological fixation that would consume an entire German army and mark the war's turning point.
slides.cap: Destroyed buildings in Stalingrad, 1942

stats.lbl: Width of Soviet-held bank at narrowest

slides.title: Rattenkrieg
slides.body: The Germans called it Rattenkrieg — Rat War. Soviet defenders contested every building, every floor, every room. Pavlov's House was held by a single platoon for 60 days — longer than it took Germany to conquer France. Snipers stalked through rubble and sewers.
slides.cap: Destroyed buildings in Stalingrad, 1942

stats.lbl: Confirmed kills by sniper Vasily Zaitsev
Of the city destroyed by fighting

slides.title: Operation Uranus
slides.body: In November 1942, Marshal Zhukov unleashed a massive pincer attack that encircled the entire German 6th Army. Field Marshal Paulus surrendered on 2 February 1943 — the first major German defeat and the moment the tide irrevocably turned.
slides.cap: Destroyed buildings in Stalingrad, 1942

markers.label: Stalingrad
markers.description: Stalingrad marks the city on the Volga where German and Soviet forces fought house by house from August 1942 to February 1943.

markers.label: Volga crossing
markers.description: The Volga crossing marks the narrow Soviet supply lifeline that kept defenders in the city connected to the east bank.

markers.label: Factory district
markers.description: The factory district marks the northern industrial area where battles for sites such as the Red October and Barrikady factories became especially brutal.

title: Battle of Kursk
sub: The Last German Offensive in the East

markers.label: Kursk
markers.description: Kursk marks the salient Germany tried to pinch off in July 1943.

markers.label: Prokhorovka
markers.description: Prokhorovka marks one of the most famous armored clashes of the battle.

markers.label: Kyiv
markers.description: After Kursk, the Red Army advanced west and retook Kyiv later in 1943.

slides.title: Kursk and the Soviet Advance
slides.cap: Soviet armor during the Battle of Kursk
slides.body:
At Kursk, Germany tried to regain the initiative with a massive armored offensive against a Soviet salient. The Red Army had prepared deep defensive belts, mines, anti-tank guns, reserves, and intelligence on German plans. After absorbing the attack, Soviet forces counterattacked and began a sustained advance west.

Kursk marked the end of Germany's ability to launch major strategic offensives in the East. From this point, the Red Army increasingly dictated the tempo, retaking Ukraine, destroying Army Group Centre in Operation Bagration, and joining the final race to Berlin.

markers.label: Omaha & Utah
markers.description: Omaha and Utah mark the American landing beaches in Normandy.

markers.label: Gold · Juno · Sword
markers.description: Gold, Juno, and Sword mark the British and Canadian landing beaches.

markers.label: Portsmouth
markers.description: Portsmouth marks one of the main embarkation ports for the invasion fleet.

slides.title: The Longest Day
slides.body: Operation Overlord was the largest seaborne invasion in history. Under Supreme Commander Eisenhower, 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel on 6 June 1944, supported by 11,000 aircraft and nearly 7,000 naval vessels. The liberation of Western Europe had begun.
slides.cap: US troops wade ashore from a Higgins boat onto Omaha Beach, June 1944

slides.title: Omaha Beach
slides.body: Omaha Beach was a bloodbath. US troops landed directly in front of fortified German positions on towering bluffs. By mid-morning casualties were so severe that General Bradley considered abandoning the beach. Small groups of survivors pressed forward and broke through.
slides.cap: US troops wade ashore from a Higgins boat onto Omaha Beach, June 1944

stats.lbl: Width of Omaha Beach assault zone

slides.title: The Liberation
slides.body: By nightfall all five beaches were secured. Paris was liberated on 25 August. By September, Allied forces had pushed to Germany's own border. D-Day proved a second front could be held — squeezing the Reich from East and West. The end was now inevitable.
slides.cap: US troops wade ashore from a Higgins boat onto Omaha Beach, June 1944

stats.lbl: Allied troops in France by August

markers.label: Auschwitz
markers.description: Auschwitz marks the Nazi camp complex liberated by Soviet forces in January 1945.

slides.title: The Nazi Death Camps
slides.body: Auschwitz became the largest concentration and extermination camp operated by Nazi Germany. Jews from across occupied Europe were deported there as part of the Holocaust.
slides.cap: The main gate of Auschwitz-Birkenau

slides.title: Liberation
slides.body: On 27 January 1945 Soviet troops entered Auschwitz and discovered thousands of starving prisoners, along with evidence of industrial-scale mass murder. Much of the world was confronted for the first time with the true scale of Nazi atrocities.
slides.cap: The main gate of Auschwitz-Birkenau

slides.title: Never Again
slides.body: The Holocaust claimed the lives of approximately six million Jews, alongside millions of other victims persecuted by the Nazi regime. Auschwitz became the enduring symbol of genocide and crimes against humanity.
slides.cap: The main gate of Auschwitz-Birkenau

markers.label: Berlin
markers.description: Berlin marks the final Soviet assault and the collapse of Nazi Germany.

slides.title: The Final Offensive
slides.body: In April 1945 the Soviet Red Army launched its final assault on Berlin. Millions of Soviet troops encircled the German capital as Nazi Germany collapsed on all fronts.
slides.cap: Soviet tanks on the way to Berlin, April 1945

stats.lbl: Soviet troops in the Berlin offensive

slides.title: Hitler's Last Days
slides.body: As Soviet forces fought street by street through Berlin, Adolf Hitler remained inside the Führerbunker beneath the Reich Chancellery. On 30 April 1945, with defeat inevitable, Hitler committed suicide.
slides.cap: Soviet tanks on the way to Berlin, April 1945

stats.lbl: Between Hitler's death and Berlin's surrender

slides.title: Victory in Europe
slides.body: Berlin surrendered on 2 May 1945. One week later Germany capitulated unconditionally. Across Europe crowds celebrated Victory in Europe Day — but the war in the Pacific still continued.
slides.cap: Soviet tanks on the way to Berlin, April 1945

markers.label: Hiroshima
markers.description: Hiroshima marks the first atomic bombing, on 6 August 1945.

markers.label: Nagasaki
markers.description: Nagasaki marks the second atomic bombing, on 9 August 1945.

slides.title: The Atomic Decision
slides.body: By summer 1945, Japan's cities were being firebombed, yet its military refused to surrender. President Truman, facing estimates of over a million Allied casualties in a land invasion of the Japanese home islands, authorised the use of a weapon unlike any before.
slides.cap: The atomic cloud rises over Nagasaki, 9 August 1945

stats.lbl: Little Boy (6 Aug) & Fat Man (9 Aug)

slides.title: Japan Surrenders
slides.body: The bomb on Hiroshima fell on 6 August. Nagasaki followed three days later. On 15 August, Emperor Hirohito broadcast Japan's surrender — the first time most Japanese had ever heard their Emperor's voice. The formal surrender was signed on the USS Missouri on 2 September 1945.
slides.cap: The atomic cloud rises over Nagasaki, 9 August 1945

stats.lbl: Japanese military deaths in the war

slides.title: The World Remade
slides.body: The Second World War cost an estimated 70–85 million lives — the deadliest conflict in human history. The United Nations was founded. Europe was divided. The atomic age had dawned. The world of 1945 bore almost no resemblance to that of 1939.
slides.cap: The atomic cloud rises over Nagasaki, 9 August 1945

stats.lbl: Total lives lost in the war

slides.title: War Summary: World War II
slides.cap: The atomic cloud rises over Nagasaki, 9 August 1945
slides.body: The Axis powers were defeated and occupied, the Holocaust was exposed, and the United States and Soviet Union emerged as rival superpowers in a transformed international order.

stats.lbl: The Axis powers were defeated and occupied, the Holocaust was exposed, and the United States and Soviet Union emerged as rival superpowers in a transformed international order.
